body:
Language and script are different

A language is a system of communication involving vocabulary, grammar and meaningful expression. A script is a system of written signs used to represent a language.

A language can exist without a written script. One script can represent several languages, and one language may be written using different scripts.

For example, Devanagari is used for Hindi, Marathi and Sanskrit. Sanskrit has also historically been written using several other regional scripts.

The Harappan script

The earliest known writing-like signs of the Indian subcontinent are associated with the Indus or Harappan Civilisation. During the Mature Harappan period, approximately 2600–1900 BCE, signs appeared on seals, sealings, pottery and other objects.

Most surviving Harappan inscriptions are short. No securely established bilingual inscription has yet provided a reliable means of interpreting the signs.

The Harappan script remains undeciphered. Consequently, the exact linguistic identity of the people who used it has not been established. Proposed relationships with Dravidian, Indo-Aryan or other languages remain unconfirmed.

Harappan writing in Gujarat

Dholavira, located on Khadir Bet in Kutch, yielded large Harappan signs made from white stone. They may originally have been attached to a wooden surface near a gateway. This discovery differs from the usual occurrence of Harappan writing on small objects.

Lothal, near the Gulf of Khambhat, yielded seals and sealings associated with its commercial and craft activities.

Brahmi script

Brahmi is one of the earliest securely deciphered scripts of ancient India. It is extensively attested in the inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka from the 3rd century BCE.

Brahmi was generally written from left to right. Its consonant signs ordinarily represented a consonant together with an inherent vowel, while additional signs represented other vowel sounds.

Over successive centuries, Brahmi developed into numerous regional forms. Most major modern Indian scripts, including Devanagari, Gujarati, Bengali-Assamese, Tamil, Kannada, Telugu and Malayalam, belong to the broader Brahmi-derived tradition.

The precise origin of Brahmi remains a subject of historical and scholarly discussion. It should not be presented as a conclusively established direct descendant of the Harappan script.

Kharosthi script

Kharosthi, also written Kharoshthi, was used principally in the northwestern parts of the Indian subcontinent, especially the Gandhara region.

Unlike Brahmi, Kharosthi was generally written from right to left. It is associated particularly with Gandhari Prakrit and occurs in inscriptions, manuscripts and coins.

The northwestern Ashokan inscriptions at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, both in present-day Pakistan, are written in Kharosthi.

Kharosthi did not produce the extensive family of modern Indian scripts that developed from Brahmi.

Languages and scripts of Ashokan inscriptions

Ashoka used inscriptions to communicate administrative and moral messages across his empire. Different languages and scripts were used according to regional linguistic conditions.

LanguageScriptAssociation
PrakritBrahmiMost Ashokan inscriptions
PrakritKharosthiNorthwestern subcontinent
GreekGreekParts of present-day Afghanistan
AramaicAramaicNorthwestern and Afghan regions

The use of different languages and scripts demonstrates that the Mauryan Empire contained diverse linguistic communities. It is incorrect to assume that all Ashokan inscriptions were written in Sanskrit or in a single script.

Decipherment of Brahmi and Kharosthi

James Prinsep played a major role in deciphering early Indian inscriptions during the 1830s. The important breakthrough in reading Ashokan Brahmi was announced in 1837, with further work and publication continuing in 1838.

Scholars compared recurring signs and words in inscriptions. They also examined later Indian scripts to understand historical changes in the shapes of letters.

For Kharosthi, bilingual Indo-Greek coins were particularly valuable because the names of rulers appeared in Greek and Kharosthi. Comparing the corresponding names helped scholars establish the values of unfamiliar signs.

Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions. Palaeography examines historical writing systems and changes in letter forms, helping scholars read and date old inscriptions and manuscripts.

Prelims focus

  • The Harappan script remains undeciphered.
  • Dholavira is associated with large Harappan signs.
  • Brahmi was generally written from left to right.
  • Kharosthi was generally written from right to left.
  • James Prinsep: decipherment of early Indian scripts, especially Brahmi in 1837–1838.
  • Trap: Prakrit is a language category; Brahmi and Kharosthi are scripts.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 35 and 39–40, and Chapter 8, pp. 79–81; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 2, pp. 28–29 and 46–47; National Mission for Manuscripts, Kriti Rakshana, April 2009–March 2010, section on Kharosthi; The Asiatic Society, Museum Collections: Inscriptions; IGNOU, BHIC-101, India: 6th Century BCE to BCE, section on Ashokan inscriptions. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

body:
How modern writing systems represent language

Many modern Indian scripts belong to the Brahmi-derived family. Although their letters have different visual forms, they share several structural features.

Most Brahmi-derived scripts are classified as abugidas, also called alphasyllabaries. In these writing systems, a consonant sign generally includes an inherent vowel. Additional vowel signs modify the vowel, while a virama or similar device can suppress it.

For example, a consonant symbol may ordinarily represent the syllable ka. Adding an appropriate vowel mark changes it to ki or ku. Suppressing the inherent vowel leaves the consonant sound k.

By contrast, in an alphabet such as the Latin script, consonants and vowels are generally represented by separate letters. In an abjad such as the Arabic writing system, consonants are the primary written signs, while short vowels may be represented through additional marks.

Important language-script associations

LanguageMajor script used
Hindi, Marathi and NepaliDevanagari
SanskritDevanagari and other regional scripts
GujaratiGujarati script
Bengali and AssameseBengali-Assamese script
Punjabi in IndiaGurmukhi
OdiaOdia script
TamilTamil script
TeluguTelugu script
KannadaKannada script
MalayalamMalayalam script
UrduPerso-Arabic script
Manipuri or MeiteiMeetei Mayek; also historically Bengali script
SantaliOl Chiki and other scripts
BodoDevanagari
SindhiPerso-Arabic and Devanagari
KonkaniDevanagari and other scripts, including Roman

Distinctive scripts and their associations

Devanagari and Gujarati

Devanagari is closely associated with Hindi, Marathi and Sanskrit. Many of its letters have a horizontal headline along their upper edge.

The Gujarati script is structurally related to Devanagari but is distinguished by the absence of the characteristic horizontal headline across its letters. Gujarati is written from left to right.

Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi

Gurmukhi is closely associated with Punjabi in India. Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, is traditionally credited with developing and standardising its use.

Punjabi in Pakistan is commonly written in Shahmukhi, a Perso-Arabic writing system. This provides an important example of a language written in different scripts.

Grantha

Grantha is a South Indian Brahmi-derived script historically used for writing Sanskrit, especially in the Tamil-speaking region.

Its use enabled Sanskrit sounds not ordinarily distinguished by the basic Tamil script to be represented more precisely.

Ol Chiki

Ol Chiki was developed by Pandit Raghunath Murmu during the first half of the 20th century for the Santali language.

Unlike most traditional Indic abugidas, Ol Chiki is an alphabet with separately represented vowel and consonant letters. It is written from left to right.

Meetei Mayek

Meetei Mayek is the traditional script associated with Meitei, also known as Manipuri. It has experienced a revival after an extended period during which the Bengali script was widely used for the language.

Writing direction

Most major Brahmi-derived Indian scripts are written from left to right. Urdu and other Perso-Arabic writing systems generally proceed from right to left.

Writing direction alone cannot establish the ancestry of a language. Hindi and Urdu are closely related Indo-Aryan languages despite their different standard scripts and writing directions.

Translation and transliteration

Translation transfers the meaning of a statement from one language into another. Transliteration represents the written form of a language using another script.

Writing a Gujarati expression using Latin letters is transliteration rather than translation if the expression remains in Gujarati.

This distinction is important in the preparation of dictionaries, multilingual documents, digital language resources and editions of historical manuscripts.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarati script: Brahmi-derived, left to right and without the characteristic Devanagari headline.
  • Gurmukhi: Punjabi and Guru Angad.
  • Grantha: historical Sanskrit writing in southern India.
  • Ol Chiki: Santali and Raghunath Murmu.
  • Meetei Mayek: Manipuri.
  • Trap: Language families and script families are separate classifications.

[Sources: Unicode Consortium, The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, Chapter 12, South and Central Asia I, sections on Devanagari, Gurmukhi, Gujarati and Tamil; Chapter 13, South and Central Asia II, sections on Meetei Mayek, Grantha and Ol Chiki; Central Institute of Indian Languages, Linguistic Resources for AI/NLP in Indian Languages, Gujarati Raw Text Corpus, Section 5.1. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: How an inherent vowel works in an abugida.

title: Modern Indian Scripts and Their Main Features

body:
Meaning of Classical Language status

India grants formal Classical Language status to languages possessing a substantial ancient textual and historical heritage.

This recognition acknowledges the historical importance of a language and encourages the preservation, documentation, translation and scholarly study of its intellectual traditions.

Classical Language status is an administrative recognition granted by the Government of India. It is different from inclusion in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution and from recognition as an official language for governmental purposes.

Evolution of the recognition criteria

The Government of India established the Classical Language category in 2004 and first granted the status to Tamil.

The original criteria included a textual or recorded history extending beyond 1,000 years, a valuable ancient literary heritage and an independent literary tradition.

In November 2005, the antiquity requirement was revised to 1,500–2,000 years. The revised framework also recognised that classical forms could differ from modern forms of a language.

On 25 July 2024, the Linguistic Experts Committee under Sahitya Akademi revised the criteria again.

Revised criteria adopted in 2024

  1. Antiquity: Early texts or documented linguistic history extending over approximately 1,500–2,000 years.
  2. Literary heritage: A substantial body of ancient writings valued across generations of speakers.
  3. Knowledge traditions: Evidence from knowledge-bearing texts, particularly prose as well as poetry, together with inscriptions and other epigraphical records.
  4. Historical distinction: The classical form and literature may differ from modern usage or may display a break in continuity with later linguistic forms.

The earlier requirement that the literary tradition must not have been borrowed from another linguistic community is no longer separately listed in the 2024 criteria. The updated criteria give explicit recognition to knowledge texts and inscriptional evidence.

Continuous use in everyday modern speech is not an essential condition for Classical Language recognition. Pali and Prakrit demonstrate that ancient intellectual and literary traditions can be recognised even when their historical forms are not widely used in ordinary contemporary conversation.

Chronology of recognition

The Ministry of Culture, in its parliamentary reply published on 2 February 2026, confirmed the following 11 Classical Languages and their recognition dates.

Classical LanguageRecognition date
Tamil12 October 2004
Sanskrit25 November 2005
Telugu31 October 2008
Kannada31 October 2008
Malayalam8 August 2013
Odia1 March 2014
Marathi4 October 2024
Pali4 October 2024
Prakrit4 October 2024
Assamese4 October 2024
Bengali4 October 2024

The Union Cabinet approved the addition of the last 5 languages on 3 October 2024. Their formal recognition dates are recorded as 4 October 2024.

At the content cutoff of 26 November 2026, the verified official list comprises these 11 languages.

Classification by language family

All 4 major literary Dravidian languages are recognised as Classical Languages: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam.

The remaining 7 recognised languages or historical language traditions belong to Indo-Aryan: Sanskrit, Odia, Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali.

Institutions and benefits

The Ministry of Culture is associated with the recognition process, while the Linguistic Experts Committee under Sahitya Akademi examines linguistic and historical evidence.

The Ministry of Education supports the promotion of recognised Classical Languages through research institutions, university programmes, awards and other measures.

Important examples include the Central Institute of Classical Tamil in Chennai and the centres for the study of Classical Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam and Odia associated with the Central Institute of Indian Languages in Mysuru.

Classical Language recognition can encourage manuscript preservation, publication, digitisation, translation and research into ancient knowledge traditions.

Gujarati and Classical Language status

Gujarati possesses a substantial historical and literary heritage and is included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. However, it is not among the 11 languages formally recognised as Classical Languages at the stated cutoff.

Similarly, Hindi is a Scheduled language and serves important official functions at the Union level, but it does not possess formal Classical Language status.

Prelims focus

  • Tamil was the first language recognised as Classical, in 2004.
  • Kannada and Telugu received recognition together in 2008.
  • The revised criteria were adopted by the Linguistic Experts Committee on 25 July 2024.
  • 5 languages were added in October 2024, taking the total from 6 to 11.
  • Gujarati and Hindi are Scheduled languages but are not recognised Classical Languages.
  • Trap: The 2005 originality criterion should not be reproduced as a separately listed requirement under the revised 2024 framework.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Cabinet Approves Conferring Status of Classical Language to Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali Languages, 3 October 2024, Release ID 2061660; Ministry of Culture, Promotion of Classical Languages, parliamentary reply published 2 February 2026, PIB Release ID 2222111; Press Information Bureau, Classical Languages of India, 27 October 2025. Consulted on 26 November 2026.]
